Doctor: I see here that you were admitted to our hospital with a history of worsening cough and phlegm production, is that correct?

Patient: Yes, that's when it started.
Doctor: I also see that you have a history of hypertension, anemia, and immunoglobulin deficiency. Did you have any chest X-rays or CT scans done?
Patient: Yes, I had a chest X-ray done but it was unremarkable. Then I had a CT scan done which showed ground glass infiltrates in the right lower lobe.
Doctor: Ah, I see. Based on the CT scan, you underwent a flexible bronchoscopy. Can you tell me what the results of that were?
Patient: The bronchoscopy showed distal right bronchus intermedius necrosis and stenosis with near-complete obstruction of distal RBI.
Doctor: I also see that there was blackish pigmentation noted in the bronchial mucosa secondary to the iron deposition given your history of aspirating the iron pill. Did you undergo any further procedures?
Patient: Yes, I had a rigid bronchoscopy for cryo-debridement of necrotic tissues with mitomycin application to the lesion. Then I had two follow-up bronchoscopies done four weeks apart which showed worsening fibrosis and stenosis of the RBI. Bronchoscopic balloon dilation was attempted with minimal improvement.
Doctor: I see. Based on the results of your tests and procedures, it seems that you have a serious condition. I will discuss your treatment options with you and your family.

Patient: I'm feeling okay, thank you.
Doctor: I see here in your medical records that you are Case 2, a 33-year-old male who tested positive for HIV in 2011. Is that correct?
Patient: Yes, that's correct.
Doctor: And you also have a history of T2DM, obesity, depression, and fatty liver disease. Can you tell me more about your symptoms related to these conditions?
Patient: Well, I've been struggling with my weight and diabetes control for a while now. And my depression has been affecting my mood and energy levels.
Doctor: I understand. It looks like your baseline BMI was 50.7 kg/m2 with a weight of 149.8 kg. But after 2 years of orlistat therapy and lifestyle intervention, your BMI decreased modestly to 48.1 kg/m2. How did you find that experience?
Patient: It was challenging, but I managed to make some changes to my diet and exercise routine. The medication helped too.
Doctor: That's good to hear. Preoperatively, your T2DM was controlled with metformin 500 mg once a day and your HbA1c was 35 mmol/mol. Is that still the case?
Patient: Yes, I'm still taking metformin and my HbA1c has been stable.
Doctor: Following 2 years of HAART for which you received Atripla (efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir) 1 tablet once a day, your CD4 count increased to 929 cells/μL from 552 cells/μL at diagnosis. And your viral load was undetectable. That's great news.
Patient: Yes, I'm relieved that the medication is working well for me.
Doctor: A laparoscopic SG was performed on you in 2013. Did you experience any complications after the surgery?
Patient: No, I didn't have any complications. I felt fine after the surgery.
Doctor: That's good to hear. T2DM was diet controlled following surgery and your HbA1c remained stable (33 mmol/mol mean). Therefore, complete diabetes remission was achieved according to American Diabetes Association (ADA) criteria. That's a significant improvement.
Patient: Yes, it was a relief to see that my diabetes was under control.
Doctor: Postoperatively, your viral load remained undetectable with a mean CD4 count of 735 cells/μL. Following clinical trial recruitment, your antiretroviral medication was adjusted in an attempt to better stabilize your mood. Did you notice any improvements in your depressive symptoms?
Patient: Yes, my mood has been more stable and my depressive symptoms have improved as well.
Doctor: That's great to hear. Your HIV status remained stable too. Based on the postoperative parameters presented in Tables and Fig., it looks like you're doing well overall. However, I do recommend that you continue to monitor your weight, diabetes, and mental health closely and follow up with your healthcare provider regularly.
Patient: Okay, I will do that. Thank you for your help, doctor.
Doctor: You're welcome. And please don't hesitate to contact us if you have any further questions or concerns. Take care. 
(Patient's family enters the room)
Family member: How is he, doctor? Is he going to be okay?
Doctor: I'm sorry to inform you that your family member has passed away due to complications related to his medical conditions. We did everything we could to provide the best care possible, but unfortunately, his condition deteriorated rapidly. Please accept our condolences and let us know if there's anything we can do to support you during this difficult time.
